answer:
**The meta-analysis (Lancet 2014, PMID 24315724)** pooled all 71,683 participants from RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE and ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (42,411 on a new oral anticoagulant, 29,272 on warfarin). It concluded that, versus warfarin, new oral anticoagulants:

- reduced stroke or systemic embolic events by 19% (RR 0·81, 95% CI 0·73–0·91; p<0·0001), mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke (0·49, 0·38–0·64; p<0·0001);
- reduced all-cause mortality (0·90, 0·85–0·95; p=0·0003);
- reduced intracranial haemorrhage (0·48, 0·39–0·59; p<0·0001);
- but increased gastrointestinal bleeding (1·25, 1·01–1·55; p=0·04).

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"New oral anticoagulants significantly reduced stroke or systemic embolic events by 19% compared with warfarin (RR 0·81, 95% CI 0·73-0·91; p<0·0001), mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke (0·49, 0·38-0·64; p<0·0001). New oral anticoagulants also significantly reduced all-cause mortality (0·90, 0·85-0·95; p=0·0003) and intracranial haemorrhage (0·48, 0·39-0·59; p<0·0001), but increased gastrointestinal bleeding (1·25, 1·01-1·55; p=0·04)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"We did a prespecified meta-analysis of all 71,683 participants included in the RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, and ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 trials."} -->

**ELDERCARE-AF (Low-Dose Edoxaban in Very Elderly Patients with Atrial Fibrillation):** In 984 elderly Japanese patients (≥80 years) with nonvalvular AF who were not appropriate candidates for standard-dose anticoagulation, randomized 1:1 to 15 mg edoxaban once daily (492) or placebo (492), the annualized rate of stroke or systemic embolism was 2.3% with edoxaban versus 6.7% with placebo (HR 0.34; 95% CI 0.19–0.61; P<0.001), and major bleeding was 3.3% versus 1.8% (HR 1.87; 95% CI 0.90–3.89; P=0.09). - No substantial between-group difference in all-cause death (9.9% edoxaban vs 10.2% placebo; HR 0.97; 95% CI 0.69–1.36).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_0e9d75e95b4aa172897de8e3f4333228","quote":"There was no substantial between-group difference in death from any cause (9.9% in the edoxaban group and 10.2% in the placebo group; hazard ratio, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.69 to 1.36)."} -->

Note on comparability: ENGAGE and the meta-analysis compare low-dose edoxaban against warfarin, whereas ELDERCARE-AF compares 15 mg edoxaban against placebo in patients deemed unsuitable for standard-dose anticoagulation — so the numbers are not directly comparable across the three.

The same document also reports that the primary outcome occurred at 1.27% per year with apixaban vs. 1.60% per year with warfarin (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.66–0.95), and death from any cause at 3.52% vs. 3.94% (HR 0.89; 95% CI 0.80–0.99).

answer:
In AVERROES (apixaban vs aspirin in 5,599 patients with atrial fibrillation at increased stroke risk for whom vitamin K antagonist therapy was unsuitable, mean follow-up 1.1 years), the hazard ratio for the primary outcome of stroke or systemic embolism with apixaban was **0.45 (95% CI, 0.32 to 0.62; P<0.001)** — 51 events (1.6% per year) with apixaban versus 113 (3.7% per year) with aspirin. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_ee77d1914d18a5ece9857b4e40a81405","quote":"There were 51 primary outcome events (1.6% per year) among patients assigned to apixaban and 113 (3.7% per year) among those assigned to aspirin (hazard ratio with apixaban, 0.45; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.32 to 0.62; P<0.001)."} -->

The trial was terminated early on the recommendation of the data and safety monitoring board, because of a clear benefit in favor of apixaban. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_ee77d1914d18a5ece9857b4e40a81405","quote":"The data and safety monitoring board recommended early termination of the study because of a clear benefit in favor of apixaban."} -->

For context, death rates were 3.5% vs 4.4% per year (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.62–1.02; P=0.07) and major bleeding 44 vs 39 cases (HR 1.13; 95% CI 0.74–1.75; P=0.57). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_ee77d1914d18a5ece9857b4e40a81405","quote":"The rates of death were 3.5% per year in the apixaban group and 4.4% per year in the aspirin group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.62 to 1.02; P=0.07)."} -->

answer:
**Primary composite outcome (CV death or HF hospitalization):**

- **DAPA-HF** (HFrEF): HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.65–0.85; P<0.001) — 16.3% vs 21.2% over a median 18.2 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 patients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85; P<0.001)"} -->
- **EMPEROR-Reduced**: HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.65–0.86; P<0.001) — 19.4% vs 24.7% over a median 16 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_b5b2f2860d0e0ed2b6663cb104221791","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 361 of 1863 patients (19.4%) in the empagliflozin group and in 462 of 1867 patients (24.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio for cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.86; P<0.001)"} -->
- **EMPEROR-Preserved** (EF >40%): HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.69–0.90; P<0.001) — 13.8% vs 17.1% over a median 26.2 months, driven mainly by fewer HF hospitalizations.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) in the empagliflozin group and in 511 of 2991 patients (17.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.69 to 0.90; P<0.001)"} -->
- **DELIVER** (EF >40%): HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.73–0.92; P<0.001) — 16.4% vs 19.5% over a median 2.3 years; worsening HF HR 0.79, CV death HR 0.88 (0.74–1.05, not significant).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients (16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001)"} -->

**Across the ejection fraction range:** the benefit is consistent. In the meta-analysis of the two mildly reduced/preserved-EF trials (12,251 participants), the composite was reduced with HR 0.80 (0.73–0.87), with consistent reductions in both components (CV death 0.88, 0.77–1.00; first HF hospitalization 0.74, 0.67–0.83).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Among 12 251 participants from DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure (hazard ratio 0·80 [95% CI 0·73-0·87]) with consistent reductions in both components"} -->
Across all five trials (21,947 participants), the composite fell to 0.77 (0.72–0.82), with treatment effects generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction."} -->

So the relative reduction is somewhat smaller at higher ejection fractions (0.74–0.75 in HFrEF vs 0.79–0.82 in mildly reduced/preserved EF), but the effect is statistically significant and directionally consistent at every point of the EF spectrum.

- **ASCEND** (15,480 adults with diabetes, no evident cardiovascular disease): serious vascular events significantly lower with aspirin — 658 (8.5%) vs 743 (9.6%); rate ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.79–0.97; P=0.01, over a mean 7.4 years. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"During a mean follow-up of 7.4 years, serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01)."} --> But major bleeding rose (314 [4.1%] vs 245 [3.2%]; rate ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.09–1.52; P=0.003), so the absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"Aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but it also caused major bleeding events. answer:
**ASPREE** (Effect of Aspirin on All-Cause Mortality in the Healthy Elderly): among 19,114 community-dwelling adults ≥70 years (≥65 for US blacks and Hispanics) without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability, randomized to 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo, all-cause mortality was higher with aspirin — 12.7 vs 11.1 events per 1000 person-years (HR 1.14; 95% CI 1.01–1.29), over a median 4.7 years and 1052 deaths.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29)."} -->
The excess was attributed primarily to cancer-related death: cancer accounted for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years, with cancer death in 3.1% on aspirin vs 2.3% on placebo (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.10–1.56).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Cancer was the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years."} -->
The authors called this result unexpected and said it should be interpreted with caution.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"In the context of previous studies, this result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution."} -->

**ARRIVE** (Use of aspirin to reduce risk of initial vascular events): in 12,546 moderate-CVD-risk patients, median 60 months, there were 321 deaths in the intention-to-treat population — 160 (2.55%) with aspirin vs 161 (2.57%) with placebo, i.e. no mortality difference.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"There were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (n=160 [2·55%] vs n=161 [2·57%] of 6276 patients in the placebo group)."} -->

answer:
## The three trials

**ARRIVE** (Lancet 2018) enrolled patients at moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event: eligible patients were aged 55 years or older for men and 60 years or older for women, with average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, or with diabetes, were excluded. 12,546 patients were enrolled at 501 sites between July 2007 and November 2016, with median follow-up of 60 months; the primary endpoint occurred in 4.29% on aspirin vs 4.48% on placebo (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.81–1.13; p=0.6038).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)."} -->

**ASPREE** (NEJM 2018) enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) who did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability, from 2010 through 2014; participants received 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo. Low-dose aspirin resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and no significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} -->

**JPPP** (JAMA 2014) was a multicenter, open-label, randomized trial of 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up for up to 6.5 years (last follow-up May 2012).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

## USPSTF recommendation (2022 statement)

Population: adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk:** the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be individual; net benefit is small, with moderate certainty, and those not at increased bleeding risk willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit (C recommendation).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->
- **Ages 60 or older:** the USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention (D recommendation), concluding with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin in this group has no net benefit.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->

## How they relate

The recommendation is built on a systematic review of aspirin for primary prevention in persons without a history of CVD, including effects on colorectal cancer incidence/mortality and harms (particularly bleeding), plus a commissioned microsimulation model stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF also commissioned a microsimulation modeling study to assess the net balance of benefits and harms from aspirin use for primary prevention of CVD and CRC, stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level."} -->

- ASPREE and JPPP fall squarely in the age group for which the USPSTF recommends against initiation — ASPREE enrolled adults ≥70 (≥65 for blacks and Hispanics), JPPP adults 60–85 — and their findings of increased major hemorrhage without a significant cardiovascular benefit in older adults align with the "no net benefit" conclusion at ≥60 years.
- ARRIVE's population (men ≥55, women ≥60, moderate risk, diabetes and high bleeding risk excluded) sits at the boundary of the two age bands: the trial's null efficacy result (HR 0.96) supports the small-net-benefit, individual-decision framing for 40–59-year-olds, but the trial's own age criteria extend into the ≥60 group, where the recommendation is against initiation. Note that ARRIVE excluded diabetes, whereas JPPP required at least one of hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes — so the trial populations differ from each other and from the broader recommended population, which includes patients not at increased bleeding risk.

## The three trials

**ARRIVE** (Lancet 2018) enrolled patients at moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event: eligible patients were aged 55 years or older for men and 60 years or older for women, with average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, or with diabetes, were excluded. 12,546 patients were enrolled at 501 sites between July 2007 and November 2016, with median follow-up of 60 months; the primary endpoint occurred in 4.29% on aspirin vs 4.48% on placebo (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.81–1.13; p=0.6038).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)."} -->

**ASPREE** (NEJM 2018) enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) who did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability, from 2010 through 2014; participants received 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo. Low-dose aspirin resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and no significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} -->

**JPPP** (JAMA 2014) was a multicenter, open-label, randomized trial of 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up for up to 6.5 years (last follow-up May 2012).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

## USPSTF recommendation (2022 statement)

Population: adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk:** the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be individual; net benefit is small, with moderate certainty, and those not at increased bleeding risk willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit (C recommendation).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->
- **Ages 60 or older:** the USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention (D recommendation), concluding with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin in this group has no net benefit.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->

## How they relate

The recommendation is built on a systematic review of aspirin for primary prevention in persons without a history of CVD, including effects on colorectal cancer incidence/mortality and harms (particularly bleeding), plus a commissioned microsimulation model stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF also commissioned a microsimulation modeling study to assess the net balance of benefits and harms from aspirin use for primary prevention of CVD and CRC, stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level."} -->

- ASPREE and JPPP fall squarely in the age group for which the USPSTF recommends against initiation — ASPREE enrolled adults ≥70 (≥65 for blacks and Hispanics), JPPP adults 60–85 — and their findings of increased major hemorrhage without a significant cardiovascular benefit in older adults align with the "no net benefit" conclusion at ≥60 years.
- ARRIVE's population (men ≥55, women ≥60, moderate risk, diabetes and high bleeding risk excluded) sits at the boundary of the two age bands: the trial's null efficacy result (HR 0.96) supports the small-net-benefit, individual-decision framing for 40–59-year-olds, but the trial's own age criteria extend into the ≥60 group, where the recommendation is against initiation. Note that ARRIVE excluded diabetes, whereas JPPP required at least one of hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes — so the trial populations differ from each other and from the broader recommended population, which includes patients not at increased bleeding risk.

answer:
Here is how major bleeding compared with warfarin in each of the four pivotal DOAC trials:

**RE-LY (dabigatran, 110 mg and 150 mg twice daily)** — Dabigatran versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation: major bleeding was 3.36% per year with warfarin, 2.71% per year with dabigatran 110 mg (P=0.003) and 3.11% per year with dabigatran 150 mg (P=0.31). So 110 mg significantly reduced major bleeding, while 150 mg was statistically no different from warfarin.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8a669b066c4cb002e5224ef48c9a8550","quote":"The rate of major bleeding was 3.36% per year in the warfarin group, as compared with 2.71% per year in the group receiving 110 mg of dabigatran (P=0.003) and 3.11% per year in the group receiving 150 mg of dabigatran (P=0.31)."} -->

**ROCKET AF (rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily)** — Rivaroxaban versus warfarin in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation: there was no significant between-group difference in the risk of major bleeding, although intracranial and fatal bleeding occurred less frequently with rivaroxaban.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8ff4bad2e9d926335b4de77ad1e41630","quote":"There was no significant between-group difference in the risk of major bleeding, although intracranial and fatal bleeding occurred less frequently in the rivaroxaban group."} -->

**ARISTOTLE (apixaban 5 mg twice daily)** — Apixaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation: major bleeding was 2.13% per year with apixaban versus 3.09% per year with warfarin (hazard ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.60 to 0.80; P<0.001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_81e343c146c92d15d7c2f15b65748ce1","quote":"The rate of major bleeding was 2.13% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 3.09% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.60 to 0.80; P<0.001)"} -->

**ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (edoxaban 60 mg and 30 mg once daily)** — Edoxaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation: the annualized rate of major bleeding was 3.43% with warfarin versus 2.75% with high-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.91; P<0.001) and 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio 0.47; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.55; P<0.001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"The annualized rate of major bleeding was 3.43% with warfarin versus 2.75% with high-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.71 to 0.91; P<0.001) and 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.55; P<0.001)."} -->

In short: significant reductions in major bleeding versus warfarin were seen with dabigatran 110 mg, apixaban, and both edoxaban doses; dabigatran 150 mg and rivaroxaban showed no significant difference in major bleeding overall (rivaroxaban with less intracranial and fatal bleeding).

Here is how major bleeding compared with warfarin in each of the four pivotal DOAC trials:

**RE-LY (dabigatran, 110 mg and 150 mg twice daily)** — Dabigatran versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation: major bleeding was 3.36% per year with warfarin, 2.71% per year with dabigatran 110 mg (P=0.003) and 3.11% per year with dabigatran 150 mg (P=0.31). So 110 mg significantly reduced major bleeding, while 150 mg was statistically no different from warfarin.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8a669b066c4cb002e5224ef48c9a8550","quote":"The rate of major bleeding was 3.36% per year in the warfarin group, as compared with 2.71% per year in the group receiving 110 mg of dabigatran (P=0.003) and 3.11% per year in the group receiving 150 mg of dabigatran (P=0.31)."} -->

**ROCKET AF (rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily)** — Rivaroxaban versus warfarin in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation: there was no significant between-group difference in the risk of major bleeding, although intracranial and fatal bleeding occurred less frequently with rivaroxaban.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8ff4bad2e9d926335b4de77ad1e41630","quote":"There was no significant between-group difference in the risk of major bleeding, although intracranial and fatal bleeding occurred less frequently in the rivaroxaban group."} -->

**ARISTOTLE (apixaban 5 mg twice daily)** — Apixaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation: major bleeding was 2.13% per year with apixaban versus 3.09% per year with warfarin (hazard ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.60 to 0.80; P<0.001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_81e343c146c92d15d7c2f15b65748ce1","quote":"The rate of major bleeding was 2.13% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 3.09% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.60 to 0.80; P<0.001)"} -->

**ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (edoxaban 60 mg and 30 mg once daily)** — Edoxaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation: the annualized rate of major bleeding was 3.43% with warfarin versus 2.75% with high-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.91; P<0.001) and 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio 0.47; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.55; P<0.001).

In short: significant reductions in major bleeding versus warfarin were seen with dabigatran 110 mg, apixaban, and both edoxaban doses; dabigatran 150 mg and rivaroxaban showed no significant difference in major bleeding overall (rivaroxaban with less intracranial and fatal bleeding).

**Meta-analysis (Ruff et al., Lancet 2014; 71,683 participants from RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48):**
- Stroke or systemic embolic events reduced 19% vs warfarin (RR 0·81, 95% CI 0·73–0·91; p<0·0001), "mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke (0·49, 0·38–0·64; p<0·0001)".
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"New oral anticoagulants significantly reduced stroke or systemic embolic events by 19% compared with warfarin (RR 0·81, 95% CI 0·73-0·91; p<0·0001), mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke (0·49, 0·38-0·64; p<0·0001)."} -->
- All-cause mortality reduced (0·90, 0·85–0·95; p=0·0003) and intracranial haemorrhage reduced (0·48, 0·39–0·59; p<0·0001), but gastrointestinal bleeding increased (1·25, 1·01–1·55; p=0·04).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"New oral anticoagulants also significantly reduced all-cause mortality (0·90, 0·85-0·95; p=0·0003) and intracranial haemorrhage (0·48, 0·39-0·59; p<0·0001), but increased gastrointestinal bleeding (1·25, 1·01-1·55; p=0·04)."} -->

**Consistency with the individual trials:**
- RE-LY (dabigatran): haemorrhagic stroke 0.38%/yr with warfarin vs 0.12%/yr (110 mg, P<0.001) and 0.10%/yr (150 mg, P<0.001) — a reduction consistent with the pooled ~51% relative reduction.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8a669b066c4cb002e5224ef48c9a8550","quote":"The rate of hemorrhagic stroke was 0.38% per year in the warfarin group, as compared with 0.12% per year with 110 mg of dabigatran (P<0.001) and 0.10% per year with 150 mg of dabigatran (P<0.001)."} -->
- ARISTOTLE (apixaban): haemorrhagic stroke 0.24%/yr vs 0.47%/yr with warfarin (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.35–0.75; P<0.001) — also consistent.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_81e343c146c92d15d7c2f15b65748ce1","quote":"The rate of hemorrhagic stroke was 0.24% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 0.47% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.35 to 0.75; P<0.001)"} -->

So yes: both trials' own haemorrhagic stroke results point the same direction as, and are of similar magnitude to, the meta-analysis's pooled estimate.

**Low-dose edoxaban in ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48** (Edoxaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation)
- Both once-daily edoxaban regimens were noninferior to warfarin for preventing stroke or systemic embolism, with significantly lower rates of bleeding and cardiovascular death.

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"an unfavorable trend with low-dose edoxaban versus warfarin (hazard ratio, 1.13; 97.5% CI, 0.96 to 1.34; P=0.10)"} -->
- Major bleeding was 1.61%/year with low-dose edoxaban versus 3.43%/year with warfarin (HR 0.47; 95% CI 0.41–0.55; P<0.001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"The annualized rate of major bleeding was 3.43% with warfarin versus 2.75% with high-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.71 to 0.91; P<0.001) and 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.55; P<0.001)."} -->

**Pooled low-dose DOAC regimens in the four-trial meta-analysis** (Comparison of the efficacy and safety of new oral anticoagulants with warfarin...)
- Prespecified meta-analysis of 71,683 participants from RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE and ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"We did a prespecified meta-analysis of all 71,683 participants included in the RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, and ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 trials."} -->
- Low-dose regimens produced overall reductions in stroke or systemic embolic events similar to warfarin (RR 1.03; 0.84–1.27; p=0.74) and a more favourable bleeding profile (0.65; 0.43–1.00; p=0.05), but significantly more ischaemic strokes (1.28; 1.02–1.60; p=0.045).

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_0e9d75e95b4aa172897de8e3f4333228","quote":"The annualized rate of stroke or systemic embolism was 2.3% in the edoxaban group and 6.7% in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.34; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.19 to 0.61; P<0.001)"} -->

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"Both once-daily regimens of edoxaban were noninferior to warfarin with respect to the prevention of stroke or systemic embolism and were associated with significantly lower rates of bleeding and death from cardiovascular causes."} -->

- Prespecified meta-analysis of 71,683 participants from RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE and ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"We did a prespecified meta-analysis of all 71,683 participants included in the RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, and ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 trials."} -->

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_0e9d75e95b4aa172897de8e3f4333228","quote":"There was no substantial between-group difference in death from any cause (9.9% in the edoxaban group and 10.2% in the placebo group; hazard ratio, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.69 to 1.36)."} -->

answer:
In AVERROES (the trial reported in "Apixaban in patients with atrial fibrillation"), apixaban 5 mg twice daily was compared with aspirin in 5,599 patients with atrial fibrillation at increased stroke risk for whom vitamin K antagonist therapy was unsuitable.

- **Hazard ratio for stroke or systemic embolism:** 0.45 (95% CI, 0.32 to 0.62; P<0.001) — 51 primary outcome events (1.6% per year) with apixaban vs. 113 (3.7% per year) with aspirin. The benefit held in a superiority design over a mean follow-up of 1.1 years.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_ee77d1914d18a5ece9857b4e40a81405","quote":"There were 51 primary outcome events (1.6% per year) among patients assigned to apixaban and 113 (3.7% per year) among those assigned to aspirin (hazard ratio with apixaban, 0.45; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.32 to 0.62; P<0.001)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_ee77d1914d18a5ece9857b4e40a81405","quote":"The primary outcome was the occurrence of stroke or systemic embolism."} -->
- **Why it ended early:** the data and safety monitoring board recommended early termination because of a clear benefit in favor of apixaban.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_ee77d1914d18a5ece9857b4e40a81405","quote":"The data and safety monitoring board recommended early termination of the study because of a clear benefit in favor of apixaban."} -->
- **Bleeding context (the condition on which the benefit was judged):** major bleeding occurred in 44 patients (1.4% per year) with apixaban vs. 39 (1.2% per year) with aspirin (HR 1.13; 95% CI, 0.74 to 1.75; P=0.57); intracranial bleeding in 11 vs. 13 cases — i.e., no significant increase.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_ee77d1914d18a5ece9857b4e40a81405","quote":"There were 44 cases of major bleeding (1.4% per year) in the apixaban group and 39 (1.2% per year) in the aspirin group (hazard ratio with apixaban, 1.13; 95% CI, 0.74 to 1.75; P=0.57); there were 11 cases of intracranial bleeding with apixaban and 13 with aspirin."} -->

Note: the hazard ratio of 0.45 applies to AVERROES (apixaban vs. aspirin); the apixaban-vs-warfarin trial ARISTOTLE is a separate study.

answer:
**Primary composite outcome (cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure):**

- **DAPA-HF** (dapagliflozin, reduced EF): HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.65–0.85; P<0.001), over a median 18.2 months — 16.3% vs 21.2% (Dapagliflozin in Patients with Heart Failure and Reduced Ejection Fraction).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 patients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85; P<0.001)"} -->

- **EMPEROR-Reduced** (empagliflozin, reduced EF): HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.65–0.86; P<0.001), over a median 16 months — 19.4% vs 24.7% (Cardiovascular and Renal Outcomes with Empagliflozin in Heart Failure).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_b5b2f2860d0e0ed2b6663cb104221791","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 361 of 1863 patients (19.4%) in the empagliflozin group and in 462 of 1867 patients (24.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio for cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.86; P<0.001)"} -->

- **EMPEROR-Preserved** (empagliflozin, preserved EF): HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.69–0.90; P<0.001), over a median 26.2 months — 13.8% vs 17.1%; the effect was mainly related to lower hospitalization for heart failure (Empagliflozin in Heart Failure with a Preserved Ejection Fraction).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) in the empagliflozin group and in 511 of 2991 patients (17.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.69 to 0.90; P<0.001)"} -->

- **DELIVER** (dapagliflozin, mildly reduced/preserved EF): HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.73–0.92; P<0.001), over a median 2.3 years — 16.4% vs 19.5%; worsening heart failure HR 0.79 (0.69–0.91), cardiovascular death HR 0.88 (0.74–1.05) (Dapagliflozin in Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients (16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001)"} -->

**Across the ejection fraction range:** yes, the benefit holds. Pooling DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved (12,251 participants), SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or first hospitalization for heart failure, HR 0.80 (0.73–0.87), with consistent reductions in both components; across all five trials (21,947 participants) the composite HR was 0.77 (0.72–0.82), and treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction (SGLT-2 inhibitors in patients with heart failure: a comprehensive meta-analysis of five randomised controlled trials).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Among 12 251 participants from DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure (hazard ratio 0·80 [95% CI 0·73-0·87])"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction."} -->

Note: the effect size is somewhat smaller at higher ejection fractions (0.74–0.75 in reduced EF vs 0.79–0.82 in preserved/mildly reduced EF), but all four trials were statistically significant and the subgroup analysis found no significant heterogeneity by ejection fraction.

answer:
**Individual trials — CV death on its own**

- **DAPA-HF** (EF ≤40%, 4744 patients): CV death was significantly reduced — 9.6% dapagliflozin vs 11.5% placebo, HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.69–0.98). The composite was 16.3% vs 21.2%, HR 0.74 (0.65–0.85); first worsening HF event 10.0% vs 13.7%, HR 0.70 (0.59–0.83). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"Death from cardiovascular causes occurred in 227 patients (9.6%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 273 patients (11.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69 to 0.98)"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"A first worsening heart failure event occurred in 237 patients (10.0%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 326 patients (13.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.59 to 0.83)."} -->
- **DELIVER** (EF >40%, 6263 patients, median 2.3 years): the composite was reduced (16.4% vs 19.5%, HR 0.82; 0.73–0.92) and worsening HF was reduced (11.8% vs 14.5%, HR 0.79; 0.69–0.91), but CV death alone was **not** significant — 7.4% vs 8.3%, HR 0.88 (0.74–1.05), CI crossing 1. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"cardiovascular death occurred in 231 patients (7.4%) and 261 patients (8.3%), respectively (hazard ratio, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.74 to 1.05)."} -->
- **EMPEROR-Preserved** (EF >40%, 5988 patients, median 26.2 months): the composite was reduced (13.8% vs 17.1%, HR 0.79; 0.69–0.90) and total HF hospitalizations were lower (407 vs 541, HR 0.73; 0.61–0.88), but the knowledge base gives no separate CV-death hazard ratio for this trial. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"Over a median of 26.2 months, a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) in the empagliflozin group and in 511 of 2991 patients (17.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.69 to 0.90; P<0.001)."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"The total number of hospitalizations for heart failure was lower in the empagliflozin group than in the placebo group (407 with empagliflozin and 541 with placebo; hazard ratio, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.61 to 0.88; P<0.001)."} -->

**Meta-analysis (five trials, 21 947 participants)**

CV death alone was significantly reduced across all five trials: HR 0.87 (0.79–0.95), alongside the composite (0.77; 0.72–0.82), first HF hospitalization (0.72; 0.67–0.78) and all-cause mortality (0.92; 0.86–0.99). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"In the broader context of the five trials of 21 947 participants, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of composite cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure (0·77 [0·72-0·82]), cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79-0·95]), first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·72 [0·67-0·78]), and all-cause mortality (0·92 [0·86-0·99])."} -->

In the prespecified HFmrEF/HFpEF pair (DELIVER + EMPEROR-Preserved, 12 251 participants), the composite fell (0.80; 0.73–0.87) and first HF hospitalization clearly fell (0.74; 0.67–0.83), while CV death was borderline — 0.88 (0.77–1.00), the CI touching 1. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Among 12 251 participants from DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure (hazard ratio 0·80 [95% CI 0·73-0·87]) with consistent reductions in both components: cardiovascular death (0·88 [0·77-1·00]) and first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·74 [0·67-0·83])."} -->

**Answer:** The benefit is consistently stronger and more certain for HF hospitalization than for CV death alone. In reduced EF (DAPA-HF) CV death was individually significant (HR 0.82), but in preserved/mildly reduced EF it was not (DELIVER HR 0.88, CI crossing 1); only when all five trials are pooled does CV death alone reach significance (HR 0.87; 0.79–0.95), whereas in the preserved-EF pair alone it remains borderline (0.88; 0.77–1.00).

answer:
Short answer: only ASCEND showed a statistically significant reduction in serious vascular events; ARRIVE, ASPREE and JPPP did not.

**ARRIVE** — no significant reduction. It randomized patients at moderate estimated risk (men ≥55, women ≥60 years, excluding high bleeding risk and diabetes). The retrieved passages give the design and background but not the event numbers, so I can't quote the effect estimate.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of aspirin versus placebo in patients with a moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->

**ASCEND** — yes, a significant reduction. In 15,480 participants with diabetes, over a mean 7.4 years, serious vascular events occurred in 8.5% on aspirin vs 9.6% on placebo (rate ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.79–0.97; P=0.01), but major bleeding was increased (4.1% vs 3.2%; rate ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.09–1.52; P=0.003), so the absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"The absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard."} -->

**ASPREE** — no significant reduction. Among 19,114 older adults, after a median 4.7 years the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 vs 11.3 events per 1000 person-years (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.83–1.08), while major hemorrhage was higher with aspirin (8.6 vs 6.2 per 1000 person-years; HR 1.38; 95% CI 1.18–1.62; P<0.001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.08)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo"} -->

**JPPP** — no reduction; the trial was stopped early for likely futility after a median 5.02 years. Fatal events were 56 in each group; nonfatal stroke 114 (aspirin) vs 108 (no aspirin); nonfatal MI 20 vs 38; undefined cerebrovascular events 3 vs 5.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The study was terminated early by the data monitoring committee after a median follow-up of 5.02 years (interquartile range, 4.55-5.33) based on likely futility."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients with an occurrence of nonfatal stroke totaled 114 in the aspirin group and 108 in the no aspirin group; of nonfatal myocardial infarction, 20 in the aspirin group and 38 in the no aspirin group; of undefined cerebrovascular events, 3 in the aspirin group and 5 in the no aspirin group."} -->

Note: ARRIVE's own event counts/effect estimate were not present in the material retrieved, so that trial's result is stated only as "no significant reduction" based on the design/background passages available.

All five sources agree that aspirin raises bleeding in primary prevention; the figures differ by population.

**ASCEND** (diabetes, no evident CVD, 15,480 participants, 100 mg daily, mean 7.4 years): major bleeding events in 314 (4.1%) on aspirin vs 245 (3.2%) on placebo, rate ratio 1.29 (95% CI 1.09–1.52; P=0.003), most of the excess being gastrointestinal and other extracranial bleeding; serious vascular events fell (8.5% vs 9.6%; RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.79–0.97). The conclusion was that absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"major bleeding events occurred in 314 participants (4.1%) in the aspirin group, as compared with 245 (3.2%) in the placebo group (rate ratio, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.09 to 1.52; P=0.003)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"The absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard."} -->

**ASPREE** (healthy elderly, 19,114 enrolled; 9525 aspirin, 9589 placebo; median 4.7 years): major hemorrhage 8.6 vs 6.2 events per 1000 person-years, hazard ratio 1.38 (95% CI 1.18–1.62; P<0.001), with no significant reduction in cardiovascular disease (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.83–1.08).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years and 6.2 events per 1000 person-years, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.18 to 1.62; P<0.001)."} -->

**ARRIVE** (moderate-risk patients; high bleeding risk and diabetes excluded): gastrointestinal bleeding events, mostly mild, in 61 (0.97%) on aspirin vs 29 (0.46%) on placebo, HR 2.11 (95% CI 1.36–3.28; p=0.0007); overall rates of serious and any adverse events were similar between groups.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Gastrointestinal bleeding events (mostly mild) occurred in 61 (0·97%) patients in the aspirin group versus 29 (0·46%) in the placebo group (HR 2·11; 95% CI 1·36-3·28; p=0·0007)."} -->

**2019 JAMA meta-analysis** (13 trials, 164,225 participants, 1,050,511 participant-years): major bleeding 23.1 per 10,000 participant-years with aspirin vs 16.4 without; HR 1.43 (95% credible interval 1.30–1.56), absolute risk increase 0.47% (95% CI 0.34%–0.62%), number needed to harm 210. **2009 collaborative meta-analysis** (six primary prevention trials, 95,000 individuals, 660,000 person-years): aspirin increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds, 0.10% vs 0.07% per year (p<0.0001), against a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% vs 0.57% per year, p=0.0001); haemorrhagic stroke 0.04% vs 0.03% per year (p=0.05).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"In the primary prevention trials, aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001)"} -->

answer:
**ASPREE** (aspirin 100 mg daily in adults ≥70 years, or ≥65 for US blacks/Hispanics, without CVD, dementia or disability): higher all-cause mortality with aspirin than placebo, attributed primarily to cancer-related death. Cancer accounted for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years; cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of the aspirin group vs 2.3% of placebo (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.10–1.56). The authors called the result unexpected and to be interpreted with caution.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death."} -->

Cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of the participants in the aspirin group and in 2.3% of those in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.56)."} -->

**ARRIVE** (moderate CVD risk, aspirin 100 mg once daily): no mortality signal — 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population, 160 (2.55%) with aspirin vs 161 (2.57%) with placebo.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"There were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (n=160 [2·55%] vs n=161 [2·57%] of 6276 patients in the placebo group)."} -->

**ASCEND** (diabetes without evident CVD, aspirin 100 mg daily): no significant difference in gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 [2.0%] vs 158 [2.0%]) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] vs 887 [11.5%]), with long-term follow-up planned; the trial's conclusion was that aspirin prevented serious vascular events but caused major bleeding, the two largely counterbalancing. ASCEND's primary outcomes were vascular events and major bleeding, not mortality or cancer.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"There was no significant difference between the aspirin group and the placebo group in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 participants [2.0%] and 158 [2.0%], respectively) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] and 887 [11.5%]); long-term follow-up for these outcomes is planned."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"Aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but it also caused major bleeding events."} -->

So: ASPREE's excess all-cause and cancer mortality is not mirrored in ARRIVE (essentially identical death rates) or ASCEND (no cancer incidence difference) — consistent with ASPREE's own caution that its finding was unexpected in the context of previous studies.

**Trial populations**

- **ARRIVE** — 12,546 patients at moderate risk of cardiovascular disease, enrolled between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, at 501 sites; randomized 1:1 to enteric-coated aspirin 100 mg daily or placebo (6270 vs 6276), median follow-up 60 months. Primary endpoint (CV death, MI, unstable angina, stroke, or TIA) occurred in 269 (4.29%) vs 281 (4.48%); HR 0.96 (95% CI 0.81–1.13; p=0.6038). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"The primary efficacy endpoint was a composite outcome of time to first occurrence of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke, or transient ischaemic attack."} -->

- **ASPREE** — community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States, aged 70 years or older (≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the US), without cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability, enrolled 2010–2014; 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} --> Aspirin did not benefit the primary endpoint of disability-free survival, with a numerically higher rate of all-cause death than placebo. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"the daily use of aspirin did not provide a benefit with regard to the primary end point of disability-free survival among older adults"} -->

- **JPPP** — 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up to 6.5 years (last follow-up May 2012); multicenter, open-label, randomized, parallel-group. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

**USPSTF recommendations and how they relate**

The recommendation applies to adults 40 years or older without signs, symptoms, or known CVD who are not at increased bleeding risk. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk:** individual decision (C recommendation); moderate certainty of a small net benefit, and those not at increased bleeding risk willing to take low-dose aspirin daily are more likely to benefit. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->
- **Ages 60 or older:** recommended against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation); moderate certainty of no net benefit. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)."} -->

answer:
## The three trials' populations

- **ARRIVE** (Lancet 2018): randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study in seven countries; eligible patients were men aged 55 or older and women aged 60 or older with average cardiovascular risk deemed **moderate** on the basis of number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, or with diabetes, were excluded. 12,546 patients enrolled between July 5, 2007 and Nov 15, 2016 at 501 sites; median follow-up 60 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors. We excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites. Median follow-up was 60 months."} -->

- **ASPREE**: enrolled from 2010 through 2014 community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged **70 or older** (or ≥65 among blacks and Hispanics in the US) with no cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability; randomised to 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"From 2010 through 2014, we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability. Participants were randomly assigned to receive 100 mg of enteric-coated aspirin or placebo."} -->

- **JPPP**: multicentre, open-label, randomised, parallel-group trial; N = 14,464 patients aged **60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus**, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up to 6.5 years.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, and were followed up for up to 6.5 years, with last follow-up in May 2012."} -->

## USPSTF recommendation and its relation to this evidence

The recommendation (JAMA 2022) applies to adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding (eg, no history of gastrointestinal ulcers, recent bleeding, other medical conditions, or use of medications that increase bleeding risk)."} -->

- **Aged 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk**: moderate certainty of a **small net benefit**; the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be an individual one, and persons not at increased bleeding risk willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit (**C recommendation**).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->

- **Aged 60 or older**: moderate certainty of **no net benefit**; the USPSTF recommends **against** initiating low-dose aspirin (**D recommendation**).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)"} -->

**Relation to the trials:** the 60-or-older recommendation is directly supported by trials enrolling that age range — ASPREE (≥70, or ≥65 for US blacks and Hispanics) and JPPP (60–85) — which found no net benefit. ARRIVE's population (men ≥55, women ≥60, moderate risk, diabetes and high bleeding risk excluded) spans the boundary: its participants fall partly in the 40–59 band and partly in the 60-or-older band, so it is only partly aligned with either recommendation. The knowledge base does not state an explicit trial-by-trial basis for the 40–59 recommendation beyond the age- and risk-defined population and the small net benefit conclusion.

answer:
**ASCEND** (Effects of Aspirin for Primary Prevention in Persons with Diabetes Mellitus):

- **Randomization:** 15,480 participants underwent randomization.
- **Aspirin dose:** 100 mg daily (or matching placebo), in adults with diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease.

## The three trials' populations

- **ARRIVE** (Lancet 2018): randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study in seven countries; eligible patients were men aged 55 or older and women aged 60 or older with average cardiovascular risk deemed **moderate** on the basis of number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, or with diabetes, were excluded. 12,546 patients enrolled between July 5, 2007 and Nov 15, 2016 at 501 sites; median follow-up 60 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors. We excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites. Median follow-up was 60 months."} -->

- **ASPREE**: enrolled from 2010 through 2014 community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged **70 or older** (or ≥65 among blacks and Hispanics in the US) with no cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability; randomised to 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"From 2010 through 2014, we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability. Participants were randomly assigned to receive 100 mg of enteric-coated aspirin or placebo."} -->

- **JPPP**: multicentre, open-label, randomised, parallel-group trial; N = 14,464 patients aged **60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus**, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up to 6.5 years.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, and were followed up for up to 6.5 years, with last follow-up in May 2012."} -->

## USPSTF recommendation and its relation to this evidence

The recommendation (JAMA 2022) applies to adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding (eg, no history of gastrointestinal ulcers, recent bleeding, other medical conditions, or use of medications that increase bleeding risk)."} -->

- **Aged 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk**: moderate certainty of a **small net benefit**; the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be an individual one, and persons not at increased bleeding risk willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit (**C recommendation**).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->

- **Aged 60 or older**: moderate certainty of **no net benefit**; the USPSTF recommends **against** initiating low-dose aspirin (**D recommendation**).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)"} -->

**Relation to the trials:** the 60-or-older recommendation is directly supported by trials enrolling that age range — ASPREE (≥70, or ≥65 for US blacks and Hispanics) and JPPP (60–85) — which found no net benefit. ARRIVE's population (men ≥55, women ≥60, moderate risk, diabetes and high bleeding risk excluded) spans the boundary: its participants fall partly in the 40–59 band and partly in the 60-or-older band, so it is only partly aligned with either recommendation. The knowledge base does not state an explicit trial-by-trial basis for the 40–59 recommendation beyond the age- and risk-defined population and the small net benefit conclusion.

answer:
Here is how major bleeding compared with warfarin in each of the four pivotal trials, as reported in the knowledge base:

**RE-LY (dabigatran, "Dabigatran versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation")**
- Major bleeding: 3.36%/year with warfarin vs 2.71%/year with dabigatran 110 mg (P=0.003) and 3.11%/year with dabigatran 150 mg (P=0.31). So 110 mg reduced major bleeding; 150 mg was not significantly different from warfarin.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8a669b066c4cb002e5224ef48c9a8550","quote":"The rate of major bleeding was 3.36% per year in the warfarin group, as compared with 2.71% per year in the group receiving 110 mg of dabigatran (P=0.003) and 3.11% per year in the group receiving 150 mg of dabigatran (P=0.31)."} -->

**ROCKET AF (rivaroxaban, "Rivaroxaban versus warfarin in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation")**
- No significant between-group difference in the risk of major bleeding, although intracranial and fatal bleeding occurred less frequently with rivaroxaban. The knowledge base does not give the numeric major-bleeding rates for this trial.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8ff4bad2e9d926335b4de77ad1e41630","quote":"There was no significant between-group difference in the risk of major bleeding, although intracranial and fatal bleeding occurred less frequently in the rivaroxaban group."} -->

**ARISTOTLE (apixaban, "Apixaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation")**
- Major bleeding: 2.13%/year with apixaban vs 3.09%/year with warfarin (HR 0.69; 95% CI 0.60–0.80; P<0.001) — significantly less bleeding with apixaban.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_81e343c146c92d15d7c2f15b65748ce1","quote":"The rate of major bleeding was 2.13% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 3.09% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.60 to 0.80; P<0.001)"} -->

**ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (edoxaban, "Edoxaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation")**
- Major bleeding: 3.43%/year with warfarin vs 2.75%/year with high-dose edoxaban (HR 0.80; 95% CI 0.71–0.91; P<0.001) and 1.61%/year with low-dose edoxaban (HR 0.47; 95% CI 0.41–0.55; P<0.001) — both edoxaban regimens had significantly lower bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"The annualized rate of major bleeding was 3.43% with warfarin versus 2.75% with high-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.71 to 0.91; P<0.001) and 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.55; P<0.001)."} -->

Summary: significantly less major bleeding than warfarin with apixaban (ARISTOTLE) and with both edoxaban doses (ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48); significantly less with dabigatran 110 mg but not 150 mg (RE-LY); and no significant difference with rivaroxaban (ROCKET AF). Note that the knowledge base does not provide the numeric major-bleeding rates for ROCKET AF.

answer:
**DAPA-HF** (dapagliflozin, reduced EF): primary composite of worsening HF or CV death occurred in 16.3% vs 21.2%, HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.65–0.85; P<0.001) over a median of 18.2 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 patients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85; P<0.001)"} -->

**EMPEROR-Reduced** (empagliflozin, reduced EF): primary composite of CV death or HF hospitalization in 19.4% vs 24.7%, HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.65–0.86; P<0.001) over a median of 16 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_b5b2f2860d0e0ed2b6663cb104221791","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 361 of 1863 patients (19.4%) in the empagliflozin group and in 462 of 1867 patients (24.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio for cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.86; P<0.001)"} -->

**EMPEROR-Preserved** (empagliflozin, EF >40%): primary composite in 13.8% vs 17.1%, HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.69–0.90; P<0.001) over a median of 26.2 months; the effect was mainly driven by lower HF hospitalization.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) in the empagliflozin group and in 511 of 2991 patients (17.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.69 to 0.90; P<0.001)"} -->

**DELIVER** (dapagliflozin, mildly reduced or preserved EF): primary outcome in 16.4% vs 19.5%, HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.73–0.92; P<0.001) over a median of 2.3 years; worsening HF HR 0.79 (0.69–0.91), CV death HR 0.88 (0.74–1.05).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients (16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001)"} -->

**Across the EF range:** Yes, the benefit holds. In the pooled meta-analysis of the two mildly reduced/preserved-EF trials (DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, 12,251 participants), the composite of CV death or first HF hospitalization was reduced, HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.73–0.87), with consistent reductions in both components.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Among 12 251 participants from DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure (hazard ratio 0·80 [95% CI 0·73-0·87]) with consistent reductions in both components"} -->

Across all five trials (21,947 participants), the composite was reduced, HR 0.77 (95% CI 0.72–0.82), and treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction."} -->

So the relative reduction is somewhat smaller at higher ejection fractions (HR ~0.74–0.75 in reduced EF vs ~0.79–0.82 in preserved/mildly reduced EF), but remains statistically significant and consistent across the EF spectrum.

- **CREDENCE** (canagliflozin): all patients had **type 2 diabetes** with albuminuric CKD — eGFR 30 to <90 ml/min/1.73 m² and albuminuria (ACR >300 to 5000 mg/g), all on RAS blockade. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"All the patients had an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 30 to <90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and albuminuria (ratio of albumin [mg] to creatinine [g], >300 to 5000) and were treated with renin-angiotensin system blockade."} -->
- **EMPA-KIDNEY** (empagliflozin): CKD with **eGFR ≥20 to <45**, or **eGFR ≥45 to <90 with ACR ≥200** — i.e. broader entry, including people without diabetes. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"We enrolled patients with chronic kidney disease who had an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of at least 20 but less than 45 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area, or who had an eGFR of at least 45 but less than 90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 with a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of at least 200."} -->
- **DAPA-CKD** (dapagliflozin): patients with CKD **regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes**, with the primary composite of ≥50% sustained eGFR decline, end-stage kidney disease, or renal/cardiovascular death. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"Among patients with chronic kidney disease, regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes, the risk of a composite of a sustained decline in the estimated GFR of at least 50%, end-stage kidney disease, or death from renal or cardiovascular causes was significantly lower with dapagliflozin than with placebo."} -->

So the three differ in stringency of kidney-function/albuminuria entry (CREDENCE required both low eGFR and marked albuminuria; EMPA-KIDNEY allowed either a low eGFR alone or a preserved eGFR with albuminuria) and in diabetes status (CREDENCE exclusively diabetic; DAPA-CKD and EMPA-KIDNEY included non-diabetic CKD).

**Consistency with and without diabetes**

- DAPA-CKD: "The effects of dapagliflozin were similar in participants with type 2 diabetes and in those without type 2 diabetes." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The effects of dapagliflozin were similar in participants with type 2 diabetes and in those without type 2 diabetes."} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY: "Results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across subgroups defined according to eGFR ranges." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"Results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across subgroups defined according to eGFR ranges."} -->
- CREDENCE: the knowledge base gives no diabetes-subgroup comparison, since every participant had type 2 diabetes; its reported result is the overall 30% relative risk reduction in the primary composite (HR 0.70; 95% CI 0.59–0.82; P=0.00001). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"The relative risk of the primary outcome was 30% lower in the canagliflozin group than in the placebo group, with event rates of 43.2 and 61.2 per 1000 patient-years, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.59 to 0.82; P = 0.00001)." -->

**Reduction in all-cause mortality:** The meta-analysis of five heart failure trials (21,947 participants) found SGLT2 inhibitors reduced all-cause mortality (HR 0·92, 95% CI 0·86–0·99), alongside reductions in cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79–0·95]) and first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·72 [0·67–0·78]).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of composite cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure (0·77 [0·72-0·82]), cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79-0·95]), first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·72 [0·67-0·78]), and all-cause mortality (0·92 [0·86-0·99])"} -->

**No significant difference in all-cause mortality:** In the empagliflozin chronic kidney disease trial, there were no significant between-group differences for death from any cause (4.5% empagliflozin vs 5.1% placebo), nor for the composite of hospitalisation for heart failure or cardiovascular death (4.0% vs 4.6%); hospitalisation from any cause was lower (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.78–0.95).

- The five-trial meta-analysis of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure reports efficacy results (e.g., composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure 0·77 [0·72–0·82]) but no adverse-event or safety-signal findings in the retrieved material. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of composite cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure (0·77 [0·72-0·82])"} -->

- CREDENCE (canagliflozin, type 2 diabetes and nephropathy): "There were no significant differences in rates of amputation or fracture." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"There were no significant differences in rates of amputation or fracture."} -->
