answer:
## Adverse events reported in heart failure trials

**Signals reported more often with SGLT2 inhibitors:**
- In EMPEROR-Preserved, "uncomplicated genital and urinary tract infections and hypotension were reported more frequently with empagliflozin." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"Uncomplicated genital and urinary tract infections and hypotension were reported more frequently with empagliflozin."} -->
- In EMPEROR-Reduced, "uncomplicated genital tract infection was reported more frequently with empagliflozin." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_b5b2f2860d0e0ed2b6663cb104221791","quote":"Uncomplicated genital tract infection was reported more frequently with empagliflozin."} -->

**Where no difference from placebo was found:**
- In DAPA-HF, "the frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal dysfunction, and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"The frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal dysfunction, and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups."} -->
- In DELIVER, "the incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"The incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups."} -->

## Adverse events reported in chronic kidney disease trials

- In EMPA-KIDNEY, "the rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"The rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups."} -->
- In CREDENCE, "there were no significant differences in rates of amputation or fracture." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"There were no significant differences in rates of amputation or fracture."} -->
- In DAPA-CKD, "the known safety profile of dapagliflozin was confirmed." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The known safety profile of dapagliflozin was confirmed."} -->

**Summary:** The consistent positive safety signal across trials was uncomplicated genital (and, in EMPEROR-Preserved, urinary tract) infection and hypotension. No difference from placebo was found for volume depletion, renal dysfunction and hypoglycemia (DAPA-HF), overall adverse events (DELIVER), serious adverse events (EMPA-KIDNEY), and amputation or fracture (CREDENCE).

## Adverse events reported in heart failure trials

**Signals reported more often with SGLT2 inhibitors:**
- In EMPEROR-Preserved, "uncomplicated genital and urinary tract infections and hypotension were reported more frequently with empagliflozin." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"Uncomplicated genital and urinary tract infections and hypotension were reported more frequently with empagliflozin."} -->
- In EMPEROR-Reduced, "uncomplicated genital tract infection was reported more frequently with empagliflozin." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_b5b2f2860d0e0ed2b6663cb104221791","quote":"Uncomplicated genital tract infection was reported more frequently with empagliflozin."} -->

**Where no difference from placebo was found:**
- In DAPA-HF, "the frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal dysfunction, and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"The frequency of adverse events related to volume depletion, renal dysfunction, and hypoglycemia did not differ between treatment groups."} -->
- In DELIVER, "the incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"The incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups."} -->

## Adverse events reported in chronic kidney disease trials

- In EMPA-KIDNEY, "the rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"The rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups."} -->
- In CREDENCE, "there were no significant differences in rates of amputation or fracture." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"There were no significant differences in rates of amputation or fracture."} -->
- In DAPA-CKD, "the known safety profile of dapagliflozin was confirmed." <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The known safety profile of dapagliflozin was confirmed."} -->

**Summary:** The consistent positive safety signal across trials was uncomplicated genital (and, in EMPEROR-Preserved, urinary tract) infection and hypotension. No difference from placebo was found for volume depletion, renal dysfunction and hypoglycemia (DAPA-HF), overall adverse events (DELIVER), serious adverse events (EMPA-KIDNEY), and amputation or fracture (CREDENCE).

answer:
**2009 collaborative meta-analysis (Lancet, individual participant data; six primary prevention trials, 95,000 people, 660,000 person-years, 3554 serious vascular events):**
- Benefit: a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001), driven mainly by about a fifth fewer non-fatal myocardial infarctions (0.18% vs 0.23% per year, p<0.0001). Stroke and vascular mortality did not differ significantly.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"In the primary prevention trials, aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001), due mainly to a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction (0.18%vs 0.23% per year, p\u003c0.0001)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"Vascular mortality did not differ significantly (0.19%vs 0.19% per year, p=0.7)."} -->
- Harm: major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds rose from 0.07% to 0.10% per year (p<0.0001) — a small absolute increase, with the same risk factors predicting coronary disease and bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p\u003c0.0001), and the main risk factors for coronary disease were also risk factors for bleeding."} -->
- Framing: net value was judged **uncertain** in primary prevention, the occlusive-event reduction needing to be weighed against the bleed increase (definite net benefit was asserted only for secondary prevention).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"In primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds."} -->

**2019 JAMA meta-analysis (13 trials, 164,225 participants, 1,050,511 participant-years; median age 62, median baseline risk 9.2%):**
- Benefit: composite cardiovascular outcome reduced, 57.1 vs 61.4 per 10,000 participant-years (HR 0.89, 95% credible interval 0.84–0.95; absolute risk reduction 0.38%; number needed to treat 265).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"Aspirin use was associated with significant reductions in the composite cardiovascular outcome compared with no aspirin (57.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 61.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265)."} -->
- Harm: major bleeding increased, 23.1 vs 16.4 per 10,000 participant-years (HR 1.43, 95% credible interval 1.30–1.56; absolute risk increase 0.47%; number needed to harm 210).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"Aspirin use was associated with an increased risk of major bleeding events compared with no aspirin (23.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 16.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210)."} -->
- Framing: it did not declare a net verdict, stating only that aspirin was associated with lower cardiovascular risk and higher major bleeding risk, information to inform patient discussions.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding. This information may inform discussions with patients about aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular events and bleeding."} -->

**Comparison:** the absolute benefit shrank from the 2009 estimate (0.57% → 0.51% per year, ~0.06%/year absolute) to the 2019 estimate (0.38% absolute risk reduction), while the bleeding harm grew from ~0.03%/year absolute in 2009 to a 0.47% absolute risk increase in 2019 — so in 2019 the absolute harm exceeded the absolute benefit (NNH 210 vs NNT 265). The 2009 paper explicitly called net value uncertain; the 2019 paper left the trade-off to be weighed by clinicians and patients rather than stating a net verdict.

- **ASPREE** — community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) who did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
- **JPPP** — 14,464 Japanese patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan, followed up to 6.5 years. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

**USPSTF recommendations and relation to that evidence**

The USPSTF population is adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk:** individual decision (C recommendation) — the net benefit is small, and those not at increased bleeding risk willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit. The Task Force concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin has a small net benefit here. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit."} -->
- **Ages 60 or older:** recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation), concluding with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin has no net benefit. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->

**How they relate:** the age-based split maps onto the trial populations — the ≥60-year "no net benefit" conclusion corresponds to the older populations studied in ASPREE (≥65/70 years, without CVD, dementia or disability) and JPPP (60–85 years with atherosclerotic risk factors), where aspirin gave no significant CVD reduction and, in ASPREE, a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} --> The 40–59 age band is not covered by these three trials as enrolled cohorts; the Task Force's assessment for that band rests on its commissioned systematic review and microsimulation modeling rather than on ARRIVE, ASPREE or JPPP specifically. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF also commissioned a microsimulation modeling study to assess the net balance of benefits and harms from aspirin use for primary prevention of CVD and CRC, stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level."} -->

- **ARRIVE** — patients at moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event; 12,546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites, with median follow-up of 60 months. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of aspirin versus placebo in patients with a moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event."} -->
- **ASPREE** — community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) who did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
- **JPPP** — 14,464 Japanese patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan, followed up to 6.5 years. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

**USPSTF recommendations and relation to that evidence**

The USPSTF population is adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk:** individual decision (C recommendation) — the net benefit is small, and those not at increased bleeding risk willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit. The Task Force concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin has a small net benefit here. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit."} -->
- **Ages 60 or older:** recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation), concluding with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin has no net benefit. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->

**How they relate:** the age-based split maps onto the trial populations — the ≥60-year "no net benefit" conclusion corresponds to the older populations studied in ASPREE (≥65/70 years, without CVD, dementia or disability) and JPPP (60–85 years with atherosclerotic risk factors), where aspirin gave no significant CVD reduction and, in ASPREE, a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} --> The 40–59 age band is not covered by these three trials as enrolled cohorts; the Task Force's assessment for that band rests on its commissioned systematic review and microsimulation modeling rather than on ARRIVE, ASPREE or JPPP specifically. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF also commissioned a microsimulation modeling study to assess the net balance of benefits and harms from aspirin use for primary prevention of CVD and CRC, stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level."} -->

answer:
**ARRIVE** (Lancet 2018) enrolled 12,546 patients with a moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event, randomised to 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo at 501 sites, with median follow-up 60 months. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"we aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of aspirin versus placebo in patients with a moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event"} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites. Median follow-up was 60 months."} -->

**ASPREE** (NEJM 2018) enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) who did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} --> In this population, low-dose aspirin produced a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and no significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} -->

**JPPP** (JAMA 2014) enrolled 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan, followed up to 6.5 years. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, and were followed up for up to 6.5 years"} --> Its 5-year primary outcome rate did not differ significantly (2.77% aspirin vs 2.96% no aspirin; HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.77–1.15; P = .54). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54)."} -->

**USPSTF** (JAMA recommendation statement) applies to adults 40 years or older without signs, symptoms, or known CVD who are not at increased bleeding risk. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} --> For adults aged 40 to 59 with a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk, the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be individual, since the net benefit is small (C recommendation); those not at increased bleeding risk and willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} --> For adults 60 years or older, the USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation), concluding with moderate certainty that it has no net benefit. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)."} --> <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->

**Relation to the evidence:** the two older-age trials are consistent with the D recommendation — JPPP found no significant reduction in cardiovascular events in patients aged 60 to 85 with atherosclerotic risk factors, and ASPREE found no significant CVD reduction plus significantly more major hemorrhage in adults ≥65/70 years. The documents retrieved do not state how the USPSTF weighed ARRIVE specifically, nor how it interpreted these trials individually, so the exact basis for the 40–59 C recommendation is not documented here.

answer:
**Populations enrolled**

- **ARRIVE** — randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in seven countries; eligible patients were men aged 55 years and older or women aged 60 years and older with average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, or with diabetes, were excluded. 12,546 patients were enrolled (aspirin 6270, placebo 6276) at 501 sites, median follow-up 60 months. (ARRIVE trial, *Lancet* 2018)
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors. We excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites."} -->

- **ASPREE** — from 2010 through 2014, community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) without cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability, randomised to 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo. (ASPREE, *NEJM* 2018)
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"From 2010 through 2014, we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability."} -->

- **JPPP** — multicenter, open-label, randomised, parallel-group trial of 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan (March 2005–June 2007), followed up to 6.5 years. (JPPP)
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The Japanese Primary Prevention Project (JPPP) was a multicenter, open-label, randomized, parallel-group trial. Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, and were followed up for up to 6.5 years, with last follow-up in May 2012."} -->

**USPSTF recommendations and their relation to this evidence** (USPSTF Recommendation Statement)

- Population: adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding (eg, no history of gastrointestinal ulcers, recent bleeding, other medical conditions, or use of medications that increase bleeding risk)."} -->
- Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk: individual decision (C recommendation); moderate certainty of small net benefit; those not at increased bleeding risk and willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one. Evidence indicates that the net benefit of aspirin use in this group is small."} -->
- Age 60 or older: recommend against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation); moderate certainty of no net benefit.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)."} -->

Relation to the trials: the three trials enrolled populations that fall largely in or above the age-60-and-older band — JPPP (60–85 years), ASPREE (≥70 years, or ≥65 for US blacks and Hispanics), and ARRIVE (men ≥55/women ≥60) — so their null-to-unfavourable results (no reduction in primary cardiovascular endpoints; in ASPREE higher all-cause mortality attributed mainly to cancer-related death) are the evidence underlying the D recommendation against initiating aspirin at 60 or older. ARRIVE and JPPP also excluded or did not include the general 40–59-year-old primary-prevention population, so they speak only indirectly to the C recommendation for ages 40–59.

The knowledge base does not state an explicit USPSTF citation of these three trials as the basis for its recommendation grades; the link above is drawn from the populations and results reported in the documents.
